Article Title: "Whatever I give her, it will never equal what she gave me": How Lamine Yamal refused to blame his mother despite childhood struggles that changed his life forever
Article Text:
Lamine Yamal's heartfelt words about his mother (Getty Images)

Why does Lamine Yamal say he has nothing to blame his mother for despite a difficult childhood?

What did Lamine Yamal say about his football style and his unexpected rise at Barcelona?

Lamine Yamal has just lifted the FIFA World Cup at 19. He celebrated with a postal code gesture, the number 304 flashed to a global audience, a quiet nod to Rocafonda, the working-class Mataró neighbourhood that raised him. Behind that celebration sits a story most football coverage has barely scratched. His mother, Sheila Ebana, had him at 16, raised him in a flat where the bedroom and kitchen shared the same walls, and worked restaurant shifts to buy him a PlayStation she could barely afford. Yamal has not forgotten a single detail.Sheila Ebana emigrated from Bata, Equatorial Guinea to Catalonia as a teenager. She became a mother at 16 while still figuring out life in a country that was not her own. She and Mounir Nasraoui separated when Lamine was three, and she chose to stay in Granollers rather than uproot him again. She kept working. She kept showing up.Yamal spoke about this directly, and without any self-pity: "I may not have had the best childhood in the world, but she made me see only the beautiful side and enjoy life. I have nothing to blame her for."That is not a polished media line. That is a 19-year-old who genuinely remembers what it felt like when his mother came home after a restaurant shift, sat with him, made food, and went back to work.He remembers the PlayStation she bought him despite how little they had. He remembers the holidays that somehow felt full.He put it plainly in a separate interview: "Whatever I give her, it will never equal what she gave me. My mother was one of my role models when I was young."The media tends to focus on Mounir Nasraoui, Yamal's father, who is loud, visible, and never misses a match. Sheila has largely stayed out of the spotlight. But inside Yamal's own telling of his story, she is the central figure. The DAZN documentary '304' makes that clear. So does every interview where he talks about his early years.When Yamal moved to La Masia at 12, Sheila stayed behind in Granollers. She kept working. She kept her life small so his could grow large. That kind of sacrifice does not get a trophy. It rarely even gets acknowledged. But Yamal acknowledges it every time someone puts a microphone near him.Before La Masia, Lamine Yamal played his first football at La Torreta, a local club near Rocafonda. The style he built there, direct, unpredictable, joy-driven, is the same one that now tortures full-backs at the highest level.He described himself in the Decoded documentary with a straightforwardness that feels almost disarming: "I'm a creative and entertaining player. I might go long minutes without touching the ball, but in a single minute I can make you enjoy watching a football match."That self-awareness matters. Plenty of teenage prodigies talk about the game in broad, rehearsed terms. Yamal understands what he actually does on a pitch and why it works. He knows his minutes of quiet are not absence; they are positioning for something decisive.He also admitted that even he did not see the Barcelona first team coming so soon: "I could imagine that I might play for Barcelona, but never this quickly. It's a dream, because from a young age you dream of playing Champions League matches."His rise has moved so fast he has rarely had the chance to absorb it. "Everything happens so fast that you don't fully think about it," he said. "Thank God, I haven't suffered any serious injury, but there are moments when you say: what a beautiful experience, because this is something anyone would wish for."Now, at 19, Sheila watches her son celebrate World Cup wins on the biggest stages in the sport. She has 200,000 followers on Instagram and around 1.5 million on TikTok. On his 18th birthday, she posted a video that said everything a mother could say: that no matter how much he grows, he will always be her little child. Yamal's response was to keep telling the world exactly who built him.
Article Summary: Lamine yamal says he has nothing to blame his mother for despite a difficult childhood. Sheila ebana emigrated from bata, equatorial guinea to catalonia as a teenager. She became a mother at 16 while still figuring out life in a country that was not her own. When yamal moved to la masia at 12, sheila stayed behind in granollers.

Article Title: Inspiring story of the day: “When I was younger they were my driving force” - How Usain Bolt turned family sacrifice into sprinting greatness
Article Text:
Inspiring story of the day: “When I was younger they were my driving force” - How Usain Bolt turned family sacrifice into sprinting greatness (Image via Getty)

How did Wellesley Bolt and Jennifer Bolt shape Usain Bolt’s career

Why did Usain Bolt’s parents stay in Sherwood Content after his success

What promise did Usain Bolt make after Wellesley Bolt’s passing

Why does Usain Bolt’s family story still inspire people around the world

Usain Bolt is remembered as the fastest man in history, but his journey began far from packed Olympic stadiums. Long before he became an eight-time Olympic gold medalist and world record holder, he was a young boy in Sherwood Content, Jamaica, who often preferred playing video games over attending track practice. Behind every milestone in his career stood his parents, Wellesley and Jennifer Bolt, whose discipline, sacrifices and support helped shape his future. Even after becoming one of the biggest names in sports, Bolt never forgot the people who believed in him first. Their influence remained a constant through his biggest victories and his hardest personal moments.Usain Bolt grew up in that small, rural community of Sherwood Content, in Trelawny Jamaica. His parents ran a local grocery shop, and at the same time they worked hard to provide for the family. Life was simple, and money was pretty limited, but they still made sure their children understood the real value of discipline along with hard work.Bolt had incredible natural speed from a young age. But staying focused was not always easy. He often tried to skip training so he could spend time playing video games with friends in nearby Falmouth.His father, Wellesley Bolt, refused to let that talent go to waste. He kept pushing his son to stay committed, while his mother, Jennifer Bolt, gave him the encouragement and emotional support he needed whenever things became difficult.Looking back at those early years, Bolt once said:“When I was younger they were my driving force. I was more focused on doing it for my country and my parents… From then on I was more careful and I sacrificed more. I wanted to use my talent in the right way.”As Bolt’s career reached new heights, he broke the world records in the 100 metres (9.58 seconds) and 200 metres (19.19 seconds) while becoming one of the most recognised athletes in the world.Despite his global fame and success, his parents chose not to leave their hometown. They continued living in Sherwood Content, and his father remained connected to the family’s local grocery shop instead of moving into a more luxurious life.That strong connection to home helped Bolt stay grounded during the biggest moments of his career. Whenever pressure built before major championships, his mother knew exactly how to calm him.Bolt recalled one conversation that stayed with him before an important race:“My mum randomly called me and said, ‘Are you OK?’ She said God told her to call me. ‘Don’t worry,’ she said, ‘You’ll be fine.’”Those simple words became another reminder that, even at the highest level of sport, family remained his biggest source of strength.In May 2025, Bolt lost his father, Wellesley Bolt. It was one of the most emotional moments of his life.While speaking before family and members of his community, he made a heartfelt promise to his mother, Jennifer Bolt. He said he would always be there for her.Bolt said:“Mom, just know that I’m here for you-fully. I’m not your husband, but I’m your child. You’re going to see more of me now than ever.”He later repeated that promise in just a few words:“Mom I got you.”The message reflected the same family values his parents had taught him throughout his life.People often remember Bolt for his Olympic medals, world records and unforgettable celebrations on the track. But his personal story shows that success was never built on talent alone.His parents handed him discipline, belief, and steady support long before the world even knew his name. Bolt has kept recognizing their part throughout his career, and he always talks with pride about where he’s from in Jamaica.His journey kind of nudges people toward the idea that accomplishments feel even heavier when they’re shared with family, the same unit that stood beside you from the start. For Bolt, the big lesson wasn’t only, running quicker than everyone else- no, it was more like never losing sight of where he came from, and also the people who helped him reach that point in the first place.
Article Summary: Usain bolt grew up in sherwood content, jamaica. His parents, wellesley and jennifer bolt, worked hard to provide for the family. He often skipped training to play video games with friends in nearby falmouth. Despite his success, his parents chose not to leave their hometown. They stayed connected to the family's local grocery shop.

Article Title: Mitch Evans has his eyes on London E-Prix despite Tokyo disappointment: “We are very much in the title fight”
Article Text:
Mitch Evans (Image credit: Instagram)

Mitch Evans has two races to claim the Formula E Season 12 title



Jaguar TCS Racing on all that went wrong at the Tokyo E-Prix



Mitch Evans is no longer the championship leader, but Jaguar TCS Racing has not lost hope despite a disappointing Tokyo E-Prix. He is just two points behind new championship leader Jake Dennis of Andretti after failing to score in Round 15 of the Tokyo double-header. A tyre puncture and a team strategy that went wrong on a rapidly drying circuit were enough to leave Evans without any points in as he was unable to finish the race. He remains hopeful of winning the Formula E title, with the team having enjoyed strong results in London in previous seasons.Tokyo E-Prix was a bittersweet weekend for Mitch Evans, who collected valuable points by finishing fourth in Round 14, but he couldn't finish the race in Round 15.Jaguar TCS Racing faced a challenging and fast-changing Round 15 in Tokyo, with heavy early rain giving way to a drying circuit that shifted the strategic picture mid-race. The team’s wet tyre pressure strategy did not work well, with the tyres losing grip and making energy management more difficult. Evans retired his Jaguar I-TYPE 7 on the final lap after an early-race brush with the wall caused a suspension issue.In a statement after the Round 15 race, he said, “We went for a full wet tyre pressure set-up today, as the forecast we were looking at suggested we’d expect a lot of rain in the opening phases of the race. Unfortunately, that didn’t come. It’s disappointing but we’re still very much in the title fight. We’ve got two races left and historically, had good performance in London, so I know as a team we won’t stop fighting.”On the other hand, Jaguar TCS Racing continues to lead the ABB FIA Teams’ World Championship with 257 points.Opening up about the issues that affected the team in Japan, Jaguar TCS Racing Team Principal Ian James said, “After a strong qualifying result from both drivers, the remainder of today (Round 15, Sunday) didn’t unfold the way we expected. We set tyre pressures on both cars for a wet race based on the conditions we anticipated, but the weather changed as the lights went out and the track dried very quickly. That put us on the back foot as the race evolved, and from that point it was impossible to stay competitive with those who had gambled on tyre pressures for a dry race. ”“But, while it’s not the result we wanted, we clearly have a very fast car in the Jaguar I-TYPE 7 and still leave Tokyo in a stronger championship position - both in the Drivers’ and Teams’ Championships - than we arrived. We’ll take that into London and keep fighting right to the end. Congratulations, though, to Porsche, who wrapped up the Manufacturers’ Championship today,” he added.The 2025/26 ABB FIA Formula E World Championship will conclude with the London E-Prix double-header on 15 and 16 August.Also read: Antonio Felix Da Costa hopeful of title despite Tokyo frustration: “It’s going to be tough, but not impossible”
Article Summary: Mitch evans is two points behind championship leader jake dennis of andretti. Evans failed to score in round 15 of the tokyo e-prix after a tyre puncture. Jaguar tcs racing continues to lead the abb fia teams’ world championship.

Bron Breakker has quickly become one of WWE ’s biggest young stars, but long before he was hitting those powerful spears and collecting championships, the Rechsteiner family had already made a noticeable mark in professional wrestling. While Breakker has shaped his own identity inside the ring, his momentum and success are still closely tied to a family that has influenced the sport for decades.Bron grew up around people who contributed to his athletic career and mindset, from a WWE Hall of Fame father to a legendary uncle and a mother who instilled a strong work ethic. Here’s a closer look at the family behind one of WWE’s brightest stars.Bron Breakker, whose real name is Bronson Rechsteiner, was born on October 24, 1997, in Woodstock, Georgia. He is the youngest son of Rick Steiner and Jayme McKenzie.His father, Rick Steiner, is one of the most respected names in wrestling history. Fans better know him as the “Dog-Faced Gremlin.” Rick built an outstanding career across WCW, WWE and several other promotions. With his younger brother Scott Steiner, he helped form the Steiner Brothers, a legendary tag team that many people still call one of the best in the whole business.Bron has often talked about how much influence his father had on him. Rather than celebrating every success, Rick constantly challenged his son to do better, which mindset helped Bron get ready for a career in professional sports.Meanwhile, his mother, Jayme McKenzie, stayed away from the wrestling spotlight, but she still mattered a lot. She played an equally big role in raising Bron and his brothers. A former softball player at Oklahoma State, she encouraged all three of her sons to stay engaged in sports, and has been credited by Bron for teaching him discipline and hard work.Long before Bron Breakker entered WWE, the Steiner name had already become famous around the world. Rick and Scott Steiner dominated tag team wrestling during the late 1980s and 1990s, winning championships in WWE, WCW, NJPW and several other promotions.Rick became known for his powerful amateur wrestling style and signature moves like the Steiner Line and Steiner Driver. Scott later rebranded himself as “Big Poppa Pump,” turned into one of WCW’s biggest stars, and eventually won the WCW World Heavyweight Championship. Their success earned them induction into the WWE Hall of Fame in 2022.Even today, the Steiner Brothers are remembered as one of the greatest tag teams in wrestling history because of their mix of strength, athletic ability and unforgettable in-ring chemistry.Unlike his father and uncle, Bron Breakker did not begin his career in professional wrestling. His first dream was football, and he spent years developing as a football player before signing with the Baltimore Ravens as an undrafted free agent in 2020. Although his NFL opportunity was short-lived, it became the turning point that led him toward WWE.Breakker joined WWE in 2021 with no professional wrestling experience. Because of his athletic background, and his natural ability, he became one of NXT’s top stars. A lot of people expected him to step in under the well-known Steiner name, but Bron decided to build his own identity as “Bron Breakker.” That choice seems to be working, because he’s already established himself as one of WWE’s more promising young talents, while also keeping the family’s wrestling tradition in his own way.
Article Summary: Bron breakker is the youngest son of rick steiner and jayme mckenzie. His father is a wwe hall of famer and one-half of the steiner brothers. His mother encouraged all three of her sons to stay engaged in sports. Bron has often talked about how much influence his father had on him.

Deebo Samuel remains a free agent with training camps already open across the league, but the silence around his market may not last much longer. Fresh reporting from CBS Sports' Jordan Dajani has named several teams circling the veteran wideout, with one AFC squad emerging as the most talked-about fit in recent days. Here's everything currently known about where the former All-Pro could end up.The Raiders have previously emerged as one of the more frequently mentioned fits. Las Vegas enters the season with a young, relatively unproven receiving corps behind 25-year-old Tre Tucker, and analysts have pointed to Samuel's physical, YAC-heavy style as a natural complement whether it's veteran Kirk Cousins or rookie Fernando Mendoza under center. His thicker frame is seen as a nice pairing with the smaller, speedier Tucker and Jalen Nailor.But the Rams, now gaining momentum, were specifically named by CBS Sports as a fit if San Francisco (Samuel's original team) has no interest in a reunion.Sean McVay's offense already features Puka Nacua and Davante Adams catching passes from reigning MVP Matthew Stafford, but the idea is that Samuel wouldn't need to be a featured piece, just a versatile chess piece for reverses and third-and-short situations.Cincinnati, Indianapolis, and the Chargers round out the broader list of potential suitors, though those conversations appear less advanced.Unlike some free agents whose markets stall due to injury or off-field concerns, Samuel's situation seems to be more about roster fit and timing than any red flags. He was a captain in San Francisco and, by most accounts, an excellent locker room presence during his lone season in Washington.At 30 years old, some teams may simply be waiting to see how camp battles shake out before committing to a veteran addition, and Samuel himself has acknowledged the free agency wait has been "tough," describing the daily routine of checking his phone for word from his agent.No specific contract demands have been reported. As an outright free agent rather than a trade candidate, any team that signs Samuel would owe nothing in draft compensation, making him a relatively low-risk depth or rotational addition for a receiver room that needs seasoning.If Las Vegas is indeed the frontrunner, Samuel would slot in as a veteran security blanket rather than a true WR1, giving whoever starts at quarterback a reliable, savvy target who can win after the catch. For a Raiders offense looking to develop young talent around Tucker and Nailor, adding a proven veteran like Samuel even at this stage of his career could provide both production and a steadying presence in the room.Nothing is finalized, and no deal has been reported. But with camps underway and Samuel insisting he's "overly prepared" for his next opportunity, a decision could come sooner rather than later, and right now, the Raiders and Rams are the two names generating the most buzz.

Article Title: “Talk to your parents”: Hamilton High School football player Khadyn Perkins dies by suicide as coach Elijah Asante shares heartfelt message
Article Text:
Khadyn Perkins and Elijah Asante (Image Via Getty)

Hamilton High School football community grieves as coach Elijah Asante pays tribute to Khadyn Perkins

Elijah Asante tells young athletes they are more important than football

The Hamilton High School community is mourning the loss of former football player Khadyn Perkins after the 19-year-old died by suicide on July 21 in San Pedro, California. Days after the tragedy, head coach Elijah Asante shared an emotional message asking young people to reach out when life feels overwhelming. He reminded his players that their lives matter far more than any game and that they never have to face difficult moments alone. The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner ruled Perkins’ death a suicide caused by traumatic injuries, with probable drowning listed as a contributing factor.Khadyn Perkins was a wide receiver and cornerback for Alexander Hamilton High School’s varsity football team in Los Angeles. He graduated in 2025 and proudly wore jersey No. 16 while playing in the CIF Los Angeles City Section Western League.According to the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner, Perkins died after jumping from a cliff near Sunken City in San Pedro on July 21. His death was officially ruled a suicide. The report listed traumatic injuries as the cause of death, while probable drowning was named as a contributing factor.The Los Angeles Fire Department responded to the area around 6:24 p.m.after receiving reports of a person in the water. Firefighters later found Perkins at the bottom of a cliff above the ocean near 500 West Paseo Del Mar. He was pronounced dead at the scene.Perkins’ death deeply affected teammates, coaches and everyone connected to Hamilton High School. Coach Elijah Asante, who returned from retirement in 2024 to rebuild the school’s football program, chose to speak directly to young athletes instead of focusing only on the loss.Following Perkins’ death, Elijah Asante shared a heartfelt message on social media, encouraging students to ask for help instead of struggling by themselves.“When life gets heavy, don’t carry it alone. Talk to your parents, talk to your coaches, talk to your teachers, talk to your teammates. There is strength and courage in asking for help. You are more important than football. You are more important than your sport. You are more important than any game, any score, or any expectation placed on you.”He also reminded young people that painful moments do not last forever.“Your future is greater than your current pain. You won’t even remember some of the things you struggle with now in the future. There are people who love you, believe in you, and will fight for you, even on the days when you don’t feel like fighting for yourself.”Asante’s words quickly became the focus of the conversation after Perkins’ death because they spoke about something much bigger than sports. His message urged students to lean on family, friends, teachers and coaches whenever life feels too difficult to handle alone.For many in the Hamilton High School community, the loss of Khadyn Perkins has become a painful reminder that mental health deserves the same attention as success on the field.
Article Summary: Khadyn perkins was a wide receiver and cornerback for alexander hamilton high school’s varsity football team in los angeles. The 19-year-old died after jumping from a cliff near sunken city in san pedro on july 21. The los angeles county medical examiner ruled perkins’ death a suicide caused by traumatic injuries, with probable drowning listed as a contributing factor.

Article Title: Inspiring story of the day: “Without the people that I have around me, all these years, without my family, without my team, it would be impossible. They give me peace of mind” - How Rafael Nadal’s fam
Article Text:
Inspiring story of the day: “Without the people that I have around me, all these years, without my family, without my team, it would be impossible. They give me peace of mind” - How Rafael Nadal’s family stood by him through every injury on his road to tennis immortality (Image via Getty)

How did Rafael Nadal overcome a career-threatening foot condition?

Why did Rafael Nadal always choose family and home over fame?

What did Rafael Nadal say about his wife and family during his injury battles?

What life lesson did Rafael Nadal learn from pain and defeat?

For years, Rafael Nadal inspired fans with his fight on the tennis court. What many people did not see was the battle he fought away from the spotlight. Long before becoming a 22-time Grand Slam champion, Nadal was told that a rare foot condition could end his career. He dealt with constant pain, serious injuries and doubts about whether he could keep playing. Yet he kept coming back. While his determination made headlines, Nadal has always said his biggest strength was the people who stood beside him. Their support helped him survive the hardest moments and build one of the greatest careers in tennis history.In 2005, Nadal won his first French Open title at just 19 years old. Soon after that breakthrough, he was diagnosed with Mueller-Weiss syndrome, a rare condition that affects the bones in the foot. Doctors warned that continuing his career at the highest level might not be possible.Instead of giving up, Nadal returned home to Manacor in Mallorca. There, he was surrounded by his father Sebastián, mother Ana María, sister Maribel and his longtime partner Mery Perelló. Their support gave him the strength to keep moving forward when his future looked uncertain.Looking back on those difficult years, Nadal once said:“Without the people that I have around me, all these years, without my family, without my team, it would be impossible.They give me peace of mind.”Despite becoming one of the biggest names in world sport, Nadal never left the place where he grew up. He stayed close to his family in Manacor and continued living the simple life that had shaped him from childhood.His uncle and longtime coach Toni Nadal taught him to stay humble, respect opponents and never believe he was bigger than the game. Those lessons stayed with him throughout his career.Rafael Nadal has often explained that returning home helped him switch off from the pressure of professional tennis. In Manacor, he was simply Rafa, spending time with friends and family. That normal life became an important part of maintaining his mental balance through the highs and lows of the sport.Nadal’s wife, Mery “Xisca” Perelló, was by his side long before he became a global star. She witnessed every comeback, every rehabilitation session and every painful setback that fans rarely saw.As injuries continued in the final years of his career, those shared sacrifices became even more meaningful. With his wife, young son and team watching from the stands, Nadal reflected on everything they had gone through together.He said:“Having my family here, my wife, my son, my team… it’s emotional because they know how hard the process has been. They have been through the good moments, but especially the tough moments during all these years of injuries.”Nadal never believed success came without suffering. Throughout his career, he played through injuries, long matches and physical pain that would have stopped many athletes. Instead of running from those challenges, he accepted them as part of the journey.That mindset became one of the biggest reasons behind his remarkable career.As Nadal explained:“If you don’t lose, you cannot enjoy the victories. You have to accept both things. I learned during my career to enjoy suffering.”His story goes far beyond Grand Slam trophies or records. It shows that true strength is not only about winning titles but also about staying grounded when life becomes difficult. Through every injury and every comeback, Nadal never lost sight of the people who mattered most. Their love gave him the peace, confidence and support to keep chasing his dreams, making his journey one of the most inspiring stories in modern sport.
Article Summary: Rafael nadal was diagnosed with a career-threatening foot condition in 2005. Doctors told him he might not be able to continue playing at the highest level. Instead of giving up, nadal returned home to manacor in mallorca. There, he was surrounded by his father sebastián, mother ana maría, sister maribel and his longtime partner mery perelló.

Article Title: A great white shark attacked a woman off Sydney; the paddleboarder who carried her to shore has now crossed 52km to win a world title in record time
Article Text:
Charlie Verco won his fourth Molokai to Oahu world championship (Instagram photo)

Police speak to people at the scene of the shark attack. (Reuters photo)

Just weeks after helping rescue a woman during a great white shark attack off Sydney's Coogee Beach, Australian paddleboarder Charlie Verco has won the world paddleboarding championship in Hawaii, setting a new race record.The 25-year-old completed the 52-kilometre Molokai to Oahu Paddleboard race in 4 hours, 18 minutes and 3 seconds on Sunday. His time broke the previous record, set by fellow Australian Matt Bevilacqua in 2019, by three minutes.The victory gave Verco his fourth world championship title and capped years of success in the event. Speaking after crossing the finish line, he said every edition of the race brings different challenges."I'm so stoked," Verco said as quoted by The Guardian. "It's always a challenge getting across the channel and each year it dishes up something different."In June, he was paddleboarding when he heard cries for help from Leah Stewart , who had been attacked by a great white shark while swimming with two friends about 30 metres from shore.The attack happened at around 11.15 am. Stewart, a teacher and mother of a young daughter, suffered severe injuries to her leg and arm but managed to stay afloat long enough to reach a paddleboard.Verco, who is also a trained surf lifesaver, was the first rescuer to reach her. He paddled towards Stewart as the shark remained nearby. "The shark surfaced, I saw its dorsal fin; it was big, about 3.5 metres," Verco said after the rescue. "I've only ever seen one shark bigger than that, and that was a tiger shark in Hawaii," he added.Verco futher described the frightening moments as he approached her. "I kept paddling towards her and the shark took her underwater and I was going, 'What do I do now?' A couple of seconds later, she popped up again."Verco said Stewart was too weak to climb onto his 5.5-metre paddleboard because of her injuries. "I had to try and keep hold of her with one hand and keep paddling towards shore with the other." He managed to get Stewart to hold onto part of the board before paddling her towards the beach, where others rushed into the water to help.Stewart received emergency treatment on the beach before being taken to a nearby rugby field. From there, she was airlifted to hospital. She later underwent five surgeries, including the amputation of one arm.The attack added to a series of serious shark incidents reported in Australian waters this year. Three spearfishing divers have been killed in shark attacks since mid-May, while a 12-year-old boy died after being attacked by a bull shark in Sydney Harbour earlier this year.After the rescue, Verco travelled to Hawaii for the Molokai to Oahu Paddleboard race, regarded as the world championship and one of the toughest tests in open-water paddleboarding.The 52-kilometre race takes competitors across the Ka'iwi Channel between the Hawaiian islands of Molokai and Oahu, where changing winds and ocean swells make conditions unpredictable.This time, Verco stayed focused on racing rather than chasing records. He finished almost 50 minutes ahead of the second-place competitor in the unlimited paddleboard category.Speaking about his race, Verco said he allowed the ocean conditions to guide his pace. "Today for the first three hours I just caught the bumps I felt like catching, and if I felt like they were going under me that was ok."Later in the race, when the conditions improved, he decided to increase his pace. "I got to three hours and the bumps started picking up again. I was like, 'Dad, should I see what I can do?' and Dad couldn't hear me because he's deaf, but George, his brother, said, 'hell yeah let's do it'."
Article Summary: Charlie verco won his fourth molokai to oahu world championship. The 25-year-old completed the 52-kilometre race in 4 hours, 18 minutes and 3 seconds. His time broke the previous record, set by fellow australian matt bevilacqua.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Kobe Bryant: "I don't want to be the next Michael Jordan, I only want to be…" - a timeless lesson on authenticity, self-belief and creating your own legacy
Article Text:
Kobe Bryant

Quote of the day by Kobe Bryant

"I don't want to be the next Michael Jordan, I only want to be Kobe Bryant"

What is the meaning behind the quote by Kobe Bryant

A real story behind this same idea

Why constant comparison can actually hold people back

Why learning from someone is different from copying them

Why authenticity tends to last longer than imitation

Why self-belief mattered so much to his career

Why every path genuinely looks different

Why this idea reaches well beyond basketball

Other memorable quotes by Kobe Bryant

"The most important thing is to try and inspire people so that they can be great in whatever they want to do."

"The moment you give up is the moment you let someone else win."

"If you're afraid to fail, then you're probably going to fail."

"I'm chasing perfection."

Why these words still inspire millions

Every generation produces someone so good that everyone who comes after them gets compared to them constantly. Kobe Bryant faced exactly that from the very start of his career, endless comparisons to Michael Jordan. He had a clear answer ready. "I don't want to be the next Michael Jordan," he said. "I only want to be Kobe Bryant. " He deeply respected Jordan and studied his game closely. What he refused to do was spend his career trying to become a copy of somebody else, even one he admired as much as he clearly admired Jordan throughout his own career.The first half of the quote is not a rejection of Jordan at all. It is Bryant recognising that even the greatest role models should inspire someone, not replace who that person actually is. The second half is where the real message sits. Wanting only to be Kobe Bryant is a statement of self-belief, a refusal to spend an entire career living in someone else's shadow no matter how talented that someone else happened to be, or how often the comparison got repeated by people around him.This exact tension shows up in an account from former NBA player John Salley, who won three championships and met Bryant early in his career.Salley has described asking the young Bryant directly whether he was going to be "the next Michael Jordan." Bryant's reply, according to Salley, was blunt. "No, I'll be the first Kobe Bryant." Salley also recalled that Bryant had studied tape of Jordan, Magic Johnson and Clyde Drexler closely to sharpen his own game, while still keeping his focus entirely on becoming his own version of great rather than someone else's replica. That small exchange, years before Bryant became one of the sport's biggest names, already contained the whole philosophy behind the quote he would keep repeating throughout his career.Comparing grades, careers and achievements is a normal human habit, and it can occasionally push someone to improve. Far more often, it just adds pressure that has nothing to do with actually getting better. Once someone measures their whole worth against another person, they tend to miss their own genuinely unique strengths. Every person's circumstances, timing and opportunities differ enough that trying to copy someone else's exact path usually gets in the way of finding your own.Successful people study those who came before them constantly. Bryant studied Jordan's footwork and mindset in real detail. Scientists build on earlier research. Entrepreneurs learn from businesses that came before theirs. None of that is the problem. The problem starts when learning turns into blind imitation instead of genuine adaptation. Real growth comes from taking what actually works from someone else and reshaping it to fit your own strengths, not simply repeating it exactly the way you first saw it done.People remember whoever brought something genuinely their own to a field, not whoever imitated someone else most convincingly. Bryant eventually became known not as a Jordan copy but as one of the greatest players in the sport's history in his own right, largely because of a work ethic and competitive mindset that became entirely his own, later known simply as the Mamba Mentality.Believing in yourself was never about assuming you are already perfect. It meant trusting your own ability to keep learning and improving. Bryant is remembered for embracing challenges directly, accepting criticism without letting it derail him, and treating setbacks as material to improve from rather than reasons to give up. That mindset let him stay focused on his own growth instead of constantly measuring himself against public comparisons, a discipline that stayed with him from his rookie season all the way through the end of his twenty-year career.Some people find success early. Others take far longer to get any recognition at all. Some overcome real hardship along the way, financial or personal. Comparing one person's story to another's usually ignores exactly these differences. Bryant's line is really an invitation to respect your own path instead of trying to force it into somebody else's shape.Although Bryant was speaking specifically about being compared to Jordan, the same lesson clearly applies everywhere. Students should not measure their entire worth against classmates. Professionals grow more by developing their own expertise than by copying a colleague. Entrepreneurs build stronger businesses when they follow their own actual vision rather than simply mirroring competitors. Whatever the field, authenticity tends to matter just as much as raw ability.Modern life practically runs on comparison, rankings, follower counts, achievements measured constantly against everyone else's. Bryant's quote offers a genuinely useful counterweight to all of that. Admiring someone should never come at the cost of your own individuality. The actual goal was never to become a copy of somebody famous. It was to find and build whatever makes you different from everyone else in the first place, a lesson Bryant carried with him from that early conversation with John Salley all the way through the rest of his career.
Article Summary: Kobe bryant faced constant comparisons to michael jordan from the start of his career. He refused to spend his career trying to become a copy of somebody else. Bryant eventually became known not as a jordan copy but as one of the greatest players in the sport's history in his own right.

A journey worth celebrating

In 2002, when Rajeev Kumar arrived in Delhi, his only goal was to earn a stable income. Armed with a diploma in massage therapy from Jodhpur University, he took up his first job, earning just Rs 100 a month. Nearly a quarter of a century later, he has travelled the world alongside some of the greatest cricketers of his generation. But the journey was anything but easy. Before becoming one of Indian cricket's most trusted support staff members, Rajeev spent years travelling in crowded Delhi buses, walking miles to save money and wondering if his dream would ever become a reality."When I first came to Delhi, everything felt overwhelming," Rajeev tells TimesofIndia.com from Southampton, where he is working with Southern Brave."I travelled by bus, walked long distances and struggled for three to four years. At that time, I never imagined I would one day work with the Indian cricket team and travel the world."Those early years tested every ounce of his resolve.He did not have a mobile phone. Someone eventually bought him a Nokia 1100 because he could not afford one himself. His first earning was just Rs 100. Stable work remained elusive for almost five years but he refused to give up.Dr Choudhary introduced him to Ashish Nehra in 2004, who used to come to a clinic in Greater Kailash for his massage sessions. It opened the doors to the Delhi District Cricket Association (DDCA) for Rajeev, who then spent nearly a decade with Delhi's Ranji Trophy team, quietly earning a reputation for his work ethic and professionalism.When the Indian Premier League (IPL) was launched in 2008, he joined the Delhi Daredevils from the inaugural season. Assignments in the ISL, Pro Kabaddi and hockey followed before the biggest break of his career arrived in 2016, when he became part of the Indian team during the T20 World Cup.What had once seemed impossible had become reality. Today, Rajeev measures success differently."Around 50 boys and girls from my village have entered this profession," he says proudly. "Some work in the IPL, some with Ranji teams, some in the Indian team, while others are in yoga and Ayurveda."For someone who once struggled to establish himself, becoming an inspiration back home means more than any medal."When people from my village meet me and say they are proud, it feels wonderful. They ask me to help more youngsters enter this profession. If I can create opportunities for them, it is a blessing."If Rajeev credits one cricketer for transforming his career, it is Ashish Nehra.Their association began while Nehra was recovering from injuries. Rajeev would spend hours treating the left-arm pacer, often on the terrace of his house because Nehra preferred sessions under the sun."When he returned to the Indian team, he never forgot me," Rajeev says. "During the 2009 IPL in South Africa, he helped me get opportunities and later recommended me for other assignments. I will always be grateful."That loyalty became the foundation of a career that eventually took him into the Indian dressing room. It was Nehra who introduced Rajeev to former India captain MS Dhoni in 2015 and in a year's time, Rajeev was in the Indian men's team dressing room.Over the next eight years, Rajeev worked alongside four Indian captains and witnessed some of the defining moments of modern Indian cricket. Each leader left a different impression.MS Dhoni's calmness immediately eased his nerves as a newcomer. The former captain regularly invited him for breakfast or dinner and ensured every member of the support staff felt valued."My first day bhai checked on me. He said: 'Tension mat lena Rajeev bhai. Bilkul chill hoke kaam karo. Kisi bhi tarah ki jaroorat ho mera kamra khula hai.' Mahi bhai took me out for dinner that day," he recalls.Virat Kohli impressed him with an obsession that bordered on relentless."I have known Virat since his Delhi days," Rajeev says. "His transformation has been unbelievable. He completely changed his lifestyle and inspired everyone around him."He still remembers Kohli playing through personal grief after the death of his father, a memory that continues to define the batter's mental strength in Rajeev's eyes."What a knock he played that day. All of us in that dressing room knew that we are witnessing something special, and it was just starting of a great career," he says."Under Virat, the Indian team's fitness went a notch above. He pushed everyone. For him fitness was everything. He was relentless. He worked so hard. I was surprised when he turned vegan, because the Virat I know used to love his food. I just want to tip my hat to the great man. What he did for Indian cricket is something that I can't explain in words," he adds.Then came Rohit Sharma , whose leadership style revolved around empathy."He speaks to every member of the support staff, asks about our families and always makes everyone feel included. Even in this year's IPL, he met and the first question he asked was about my family."Then came the young captain Shubman Gill , whose majestic form helped India draw the five-match Test series in England in 2025. It was also Rajeev's last series with the Indian team."Very sweet boy with a very good head on his shoulder. He has got the best of Mahi bhai, Virat, and Rohit. He has only shown glimpses of his excellent leadership skills. He will take Indian cricket to greater heights," says Rajeev.For Rajeev, those qualities mattered as much as tactical acumen.Life inside the Indian dressing room was built on relationships that extended beyond the boundary rope.During the Covid-19 pandemic, Rajeev's younger son fell seriously ill. What followed remains one of the most emotional chapters of his career."The entire Indian team stood by me," he says. "The players kept calling to ask about my family and even offered financial support. I can never forget that."Those gestures reinforced what he already believed about the group he served for years.Rajeev experienced cricket's cruelest moments from the closest quarters. He remembers the devastation after India's semifinal exit in the 2016 T20 World Cup. But nothing matched the silence inside the dressing room after the 2023 ODI World Cup final in Ahmedabad."Everyone was emotional. It was my first stint with the team and I felt so bad.(Everyone was so down) " he recalls."Then that night in Ahmedabad. Agar mera bas chale toh mai November 19 ko hata do (I want to eradicate memories of November 19). The dressing room was heartbroken."Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit after the defeat, he says, offered words of encouragement when the squad needed them most.As South Africa closed in during the final of the 2024 T20 World Cup, Rajeev admits he could do little except pray."When they needed around 30 runs towards the end, I was sitting quietly near the boundary praying for a miracle.(Please god not again)."The miracle arrived. India became world champions."For me, it felt like years of hard work had finally been rewarded."Away from the spotlight, the dressing room had its lighter moments too.Mohammed Siraj, Mohammed Shami and Kuldeep Yadav were among the regular visitors seeking treatment, but Kuldeep stood out."We used to joke that Kuldeep deserved an award because he probably took the most massages," Rajeev says with a laugh.His bond with Rishabh Pant was equally special. When Pant had his horrific car accident, Rajeev rushed to a Hanuman temple with his family to pray."Looking at the accident, we feared the worst," he says. "Thankfully, he recovered. He is a wonderful person who always helps others."Rajeev Kumar 's story is not merely about working alongside cricket's biggest stars.It is about a young man from a small village who arrived in Delhi with almost nothing, endured years of uncertainty, embraced education when sports science was still finding its feet in Indian cricket, and quietly became one of the most trusted figures behind the scenes.His hands helped players recover, but his own journey was built on resilience, humility and gratitude.From earning Rs 100 to celebrating a World Cup triumph on the biggest stage, Rajeev Kumar's greatest achievement may not be the medals he collected along the way. It is proving that even the quietest journeys can leave the loudest impact.
